title: LYNX - A trapped-ion quantum information processor
authors: Alexander Erhard, Georg Jacob, Max Hettrich, Philip C. Holz, Juris Ulmanis, Thomas Feldker
abstract: We introduce LYNX, a quantum information processor based on trapped $^{40}$Ca$^+$ ions. It utilizes up to 31 qubits with all-to-all connectivity. We characterize the system performance using rigorous benchmarks, such as randomized benchmarking (RB), GHZ state fidelity estimates, and quantum volume (QV) tests. The LYNX processor shows average 1-qubit gate errors of $8(5)\times 10^{-5}$ tested via standard RB in a 24-qubit register. An average 2-qubit gate error in a 24-qubit register of $2.84(8)\times 10^{-3}$ is demonstrated using interleaved RB. Furthermore, the device passes QV tests using up to 15 qubits which corresponds to a quantum volume of QV$=2^{15}$.
summary: This paper introduces LYNX, a quantum processor built with trapped $^{40}	ext{Ca}^+$ ions, demonstrating its capability to handle up to 31 qubits with full connectivity. The authors rigorously benchmarked the system using advanced techniques, achieving low gate error rates and confirming high-fidelity entanglement up to 15 qubits. The results solidify trapped ions as a powerful, scalable platform for quantum computation.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop and rigorously characterize a scalable quantum information processor using trapped ions.
main_result: The LYNX processor demonstrated low error rates for both 1-qubit ($\sim 10^{-4}$) and 2-qubit ($\sim 10^{-3}$) gates, and successfully passed Quantum Volume tests up to 15 qubits, confirming genuine multi-particle entanglement.
method: Performance was benchmarked using Randomized Benchmarking (RB) for gate errors, GHZ state fidelity measurements, and Quantum Volume (QV) tests.
model_or_system: The system is LYNX, a quantum processor based on trapped $^{40}	ext{Ca}^+$ ions, capable of hosting up to 31 qubits with all-to-all connectivity. Qubits are encoded in the Zeeman states of the $^{42}	ext{S}_{1/2}$ ground state.

important_parameters: Gate durations ($T_{1q} \sim 90 \mu	ext{s}$, $T_{2q} \sim 210 \mu	ext{s}$), coherence times ($T_1 \approx 10 	ext{ s}$), and qubit count (up to 31).
main_assumptions: The 1-qubit gate sequence is decomposed into a product of simpler gates, and the performance metrics are derived from standard benchmarking protocols.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate 1-qubit RB results on the 31-qubit register, the distribution of 2-qubit gate errors, parity oscillations for the 31-qubit GHZ state, and the successful passing of QV tests for 15 qubits.
paper_structure: The paper details the physical implementation using trapped ions, describes the native gate set and their mathematical definitions, presents the experimental benchmarking procedures (RB, GHZ, QV), and concludes with the measured performance metrics.
why_interesting: This work provides concrete, high-fidelity experimental benchmarks for a leading physical platform (trapped ions) in quantum computing, directly relevant to understanding error mitigation and scaling in quantum information processing.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Illustrationa of the LYNX setup. Ions are trapped in an AQT PINE linear Paul trap. In the PINE trap N ions can be stored in a static linear arrangement, forming a quantum register. Arbitrary resonant rotations R(θ, ϕ) on the qubits are performed by an RF field, that is created by an antenna, interacting collectively with all qubits. A tightly focused laser beam at 405 nm wavelength that can be steered on individual ions is utilized to perform addressed Rz(θ)i rotations on an individual qubit i. The diagonal entries show the error of the active qubits on which RB is performed, whereas off-diagonal entries show errors on idling qubits during the sequence. Se- quences comprising up to 400 Cliffords are performed, where the estimated average error per Clifford gate for the active qubits is ϵ1q = 1.6(2) × 10−4.
